header:
Date: 2027-12-10
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 56m
Attendees: Sam Lane (Redwood AE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Devin Ortiz (Redwood CSM), Aisha Khan (MarinerPay SRE), Tom Reynolds (MarinerPay CTO), Marta Gonzalez (Product), Eli Wu (Engineer)
summary: Postmortem follow-up focused on a repeated fallback loop that increased latency and caused token-cost spikes during peak batch windows. Agreed immediate mitigations (circuit-breaker + stricter canary thresholds), telemetry sharing, and a joint runbook rehearsal later this month.
topics: Incident timeline recap, root-cause hypothesis (cache eviction + autoscaler ripple), mitigation options (circuit breaker, prioritized KV cache warming, throttling), rollout plan for hardened fallback, monitoring & alerting thresholds, compliance/trace access, next steps and owners.
transcript:
[00:00] Sam Lane: ok hi everyone thanks for joining on short notice um this is the bridgecall to walk through the fallback loop postmortem and next steps, we'll try to keep to 45 minutes but we've got 56 booked so that's fine
[00:22] Aisha Khan: hey yeah thanks, last week at 10:22 UTC we saw a sustained latency increase, the service started bouncing to the smaller model and then that caused request pileup and the autoscaler overshot, we ended up in a loop for about 18 minutes
[00:45] Priya Rao: yep and our traces show a repeated sequence where the KV cache misses were spiking after a scale event, then prefix cache warming lagged, token generation slowed and the routing policy kicked fallback to the cheaper model which was slower under this pattern - weird coupling
[01:10] Tom Reynolds: just to be clear, it wasn't a single model failure it was an interaction between scaling, cache and our throttles?
[01:22] Speaker 6: (inaudible) ... yeah that looks right
[01:30] Priya Rao: correct, our hypothesis is twofold: first, the autoscaler reaction window is too permissive for bursty seq lengths; second, the KV cache eviction policy on your workload pattern is evicting hot prefixes during scale down and rebuilds are expensive
[01:52] Marta Gonzalez: can you explain why fallback made it worse? I thought fallback was supposed to be safer
[02:05] Sam Lane: good Q, fallback in this case chose a model variant with smaller concurrency but lower throughput for long sequences. The routing policy saw higher p95 so it moved traffic, which increased per-request latency under load and caused more backlog which cascaded back into scaling decisions
[02:30] Eli Wu: so it's like, we switched to a smaller engine and that engine gets saturated quicker leading to longer queues?
[02:40] Priya Rao: yes exactly and the runtime's backpressure signals were interpreted by your autoscaler as higher latency, so it added more instances which then caused new cold KV caches and the loop repeated
[02:58] Aisha Khan: we also noticed spikes in token-cost during the event — the generated tokens jumped because retries and longer sequences piled up
[03:15] Devin Ortiz: on the customer success side we want to minimize these economic impacts and the user-visible latency — so the mitigation needs to address both the control loop and the cold-cache rebuild
[03:33] Sam Lane: proposed immediate mitigations: 1) temporary circuit-breaker on fallback transitions (delay repeated fallback within a 2m window), 2) adjust autoscaler sensitivity to prefer steady-state vs transient spikes, 3) pre-warm KV cache during scale events for known hot prefixes, 4) throttle ingress at edge for long sequence requests when system enters degraded state
[03:58] Tom Reynolds: number 1 seems high value quick win, what's the implementation effort?
[04:10] Priya Rao: we can push a config change to your routing policy from our side — it's config-only for hosted, for Private we'd provide the policy diff. It should be low risk and rollbackable
[04:25] Aisha Khan: will that require downtime?
[04:30] Sam Lane: no downtime. It's a config toggle, we can canary it across a small subset of traffic first
[04:40] Marta Gonzalez: who owns the canary? will Redwood run it or do we need to coordinate?
[04:45] Devin Ortiz: we'll run it jointly — Redwood will apply and MarinerPay will monitor and validate metrics
[04:50] [08:10] Priya Rao: (note: jumped ahead) we looked at traces attached in the doc, the problematic window shows consistent 500ms-1s cold cache penalties per request during rebuilds, that multiplied across 2000 concurrent reqs
[08:30] Aisha Khan: we uploaded additional logs to the shared folder, you might see some naming artifacts, our prod cluster uses an internal service name that the transcript sometimes obfuscates
[08:45] Sam Lane: thanks, we'll correlate. One more lower-risk mitigation: implement a soft-priority queue that favors short sequences and critical routes during degraded modes — reduces tail latency for interactive customers
[09:10] Eli Wu: that's interesting, how intrusive is that?
[09:20] Priya Rao: it's a runtime policy change and requires routing rules + a small client header that tags request priority. We can fall back to default if client tag is missing so it's backwards compatible
[09:38] Tom Reynolds: ok sounds plausible. What about observability — we need clear alarms so we don't get surprised again
[09:48] Sam Lane: agreed, action on alarms: add a combined alert that fires when p95 > threshold AND KV cache hitrate drops below X% for >5m. That avoids noise from transient blips
[10:05] Aisha Khan: would like that to be in our pager duty playbook too
[10:12] Devin Ortiz: we'll update the runbook and index the alert with suggested remediation steps (rollback canary, increase min replicas, enable KV pre-warm)
[10:25] [15:00] Marta Gonzalez: compliance question — for the traces we need access patterns and we need to keep PI redacted, can Redwood grant scoped trace access to our security team?
[15:12] Sam Lane: yes, we can provide time-limited, read-only trace links and mask PII. For Private deployments we can assist with audit log exports but for hosted we'll provide scrubbed artifacts per our SOC 2 process
[15:35] Tom Reynolds: will this require a legal addendum?
[15:40] Devin Ortiz: not for this scoped access; if you want raw traces with customer headers preserved we might need a DPA addendum — we'll confirm with legal and send guidance
[16:02] Priya Rao: back to technicals: longer-term mitigations we discussed — improve autoscaler hysteresis, add model fallback throttling with exponential backoff, smarter KV eviction tuned to seq length distribution, and preemptive quantization options for peak windows to reduce GPU latency
[16:30] Eli Wu: quantization seems heavy handed — will it change outputs quality?
[16:38] Priya Rao: there's tradeoff; we can suggest per-route quantization and run A/B with your eval set before rolling out broadly. Redwood Optimize has a profile engine to simulate token-level quality delta
[16:55] Aisha Khan: what's the estimated timeline for the config-only mitigations?
[17:05] Sam Lane: circuit-breaker config + alerting tweaks can be done in 48-72 hours, the pre-warm scripts and runbook we'll aim for 1 week, runtime policy + client tagging for priority queue 2-3 weeks depending on coordination
[17:20] Marta Gonzalez: ok, we'll need to brief engineering leadership — can you summarize the proposed canary plan?
[17:30] Sam Lane: yes, brief: 1) Apply circuit-breaker config to 5% traffic, 2) Monitor p95 and cache hitrate for 24 hours, 3) If stable expand to 25% then 100% over 48h, rollback if combined alert fires. We'll add telemetry dashboards for each step
[17:55] [22:00] Tom Reynolds: what about cost impact, you mentioned token-cost spike earlier — will these mitigations save money?
[22:12] Priya Rao: immediate savings come from avoiding retry storms and repeated long-inference runs — circuit-breaker reduces duplicate work. Pre-warm avoids wasted tokens during rebuilds. Quantization helps but needs careful eval
[22:33] Aisha Khan: any specific numbers?
[22:36] Sam Lane: rough estimate from similar customers: fallback-loop remediations can reduce incident token expenditure by 30-60% on affected windows; we'll produce modelled spreadsheet after we ingest your telemetry
[22:55] Marta Gonzalez: great. Are there any blockers on Redwood side for the 48-72h config roll?
[23:05] Priya Rao: none, but we'll need approval to deploy the routing config to your live tenant; please confirm the maintenance window if you have change controls
[23:20] Aisha Khan: we can approve an out-of-hours window tonight if needed, but prefer tomorrow morning UTC 07:00
[23:35] Devin Ortiz: we'll respect your window — Sam and Priya will coordinate and post the runbook; I'll own the comms thread
[23:48] Sam Lane: ok action recaps: Sam will share trace links + canary config; Priya will share circuit-breaker policy and proposed backoff; Devin will publish runbook; Aisha will run load script and provide telemetry. Dates noted in action items
[24:10] Eli Wu: small nit — in the uploaded trace a lot of hostnames got turned into generic tokens in the auto transcript so we might need manual correlation to our internal ids
[24:25] Priya Rao: yep we'll annotate traces with your ids if you provide mapping file
[24:40] Tom Reynolds: any change to SLAs or credits?
[24:48] Devin Ortiz: not part of this session, we'll route to account team; if the incident meets SLA violation thresholds we'll escalate per contract
[25:05] [30:00] Sam Lane: ok I think that's everything, we'll follow up with the artifacts. Thanks all for quick action here
[30:15] Aisha Khan: thanks everyone, appreciate the concrete plan
[30:22] Marta Gonzalez: will there be a dry-run/rehearsal?
[30:30] Devin Ortiz: yes week of 2027-12-20 we'll run a joint rehearsal of the runbook under simulated load
[30:40] Sam Lane: and we'll put a short postmortem doc into the shared folder after the canary completes
[30:50] [END]
